---
title: The Environment
---

A script can print `$HOME` and get the right answer, although nothing in the
script ever set it. Values like that reach a program through the
**environment**: a list of names and values that the shell hands to everything
it starts.

Your own variables are not on that list, and this chapter is about the
difference.

In this chapter, we'll learn how to:

* see what a script inherits and what it does not
* put a variable in the environment with `export`
* set a value for one command only

And the one idea to hold on to from the start: **a variable belongs to the
shell you set it in; only the environment travels.**

## What a script inherits

Here is a script that prints three variables, one of which is our own:

```{.bash filename="show.sh"}
echo "HOME is $HOME"
echo "USER is $USER"
echo "name is $name"
```

```session
$ bash show.sh
HOME is /home/anand
USER is anand
name is
```

Two of the three worked. The third, `name`, is empty - and it is empty even if
you set it a moment before:

```session
$ name=alice
```

```session
$ bash show.sh
HOME is /home/anand
USER is anand
name is
```

The variable is certainly set. Ask the shell you are typing in and it will tell
you so:

```session
$ echo $name
alice
```

So `HOME` reached the script and `name` did not.

`HOME` and `USER` are in the environment, which is how the script saw them.
Every program gets that list - `date`, `figlet`, your script, and the shell
itself when you logged in. They are not shell settings; they are how the system
tells every program on the machine who you are and where your files live.

Your own variables are not in the list. A variable you set belongs to the shell
you set it in, and to nothing else. `bash show.sh` starts a second shell to run
the script, and that shell was handed the environment, not your variables.

::: {.callout-note}
The command `env` prints the whole environment. It is a long list on most
machines, and most of it is not addressed to you - it is settings that programs
put there for other programs.
:::

## export

To put a variable in the environment, mark it with `export`:

```session
$ export name
```

```session
$ bash show.sh
HOME is /home/anand
USER is anand
name is alice
```

Nothing about `name` changed. It held `alice` before and it holds `alice` now.
What changed is that it now travels: every program this shell starts from here
on will be handed it.

Marking and setting can be done in one line, which is how you will usually see
it written:

```session
$ export name=alice
```

`export` is one-way and it is not permanent. It affects the shell you type it
in and the programs that shell starts. Close the terminal and it is gone, along
with the shell that held it.

## For one command only

Sometimes a program needs a value once and you do not want to change your shell
at all. Write the assignment in front of the command:

```session
$ name=bob bash show.sh
HOME is /home/anand
USER is anand
name is bob
```

The script saw `bob`. And your own `name` is untouched:

```session
$ echo $name
alice
```

This is how you try a program with a different setting without living with the
consequences of it.

## Summary

| What you write | What it means |
|----------------|---------------|
| the environment | a list of names and values handed to every program the shell starts |
| `x=5` | sets `x` in this shell only; programs it starts will not see it |
| `export x` | puts `x` in the environment, so programs started from here get it |
| `export x=5` | sets it and exports it in one line |
| `x=5 somecmd` | runs `somecmd` with `x` set to `5`, and leaves this shell alone |
| `env` | prints the whole environment |

And the one idea to carry forward: a variable belongs to the shell it was set
in. Only what has been exported into the environment reaches the programs that
shell starts.
